title: 7 Habits of Highly Effective Generative AI Evaluations - Justin Muller
talk_summary: An AWS applied-AI architect argues that the missing piece to scaling GenAI workloads is a fast, explainable, segmented evaluation framework whose primary goal is discovering problems rather than producing a single quality score. He gives seven habits (fast, quantifiable, explainable, segmented, diverse, traditional, gold-standard) and shows a document-processing customer going from 22% to 92% accuracy once evals existed.

takeaways.what_they_do: Design the eval harness to surface where and why the system fails (with judge reasoning and per-category summaries), not just to emit a pass/fail number.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The main goal with any evaluation framework should be to discover problems.
takeaways.numbers: Customer went 22% -> 92% accuracy after building evals; 90% was launch threshold

takeaways.what_they_do: Run ~100 test cases in parallel for generation (~10s), judge them in parallel (~10s), then summarize by category (~10s) so a prompt change can be validated in seconds, enabling hundreds of iterations per day.

takeaways.technique: Gold standard set built by humans, not the model
takeaways.what_they_do: Invest heavily in a human-curated gold set; use GenAI only for a 'silver' draft that a human reviews, because errors in the gold set propagate into the whole system.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this is a a terrible place to use GEI. If you use GEI to create your gold standard set

takeaways.what_they_do: Engineer the judge prompt like a grading rubric (explicit criteria and deductions) and require the judge to output its reasoning alongside the score.
takeaways.evidence_quote: asking your judge to explain its reasoning is often a good way to uh do prompt engineering for the judge

takeaways.technique: Prompt decomposition / semantic routing to cut dead tokens
takeaways.what_they_do: Split a large multi-instruction prompt into chained steps, route easy vs hard inputs to small vs large models, and eval each step; removes 'dead space' instructions and lets deterministic steps use Python.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Those hard instructions are basically dead space. They weren't necessary, but what they are is extra cost
takeaways.numbers: Weather customer hit 100% accuracy after moving numeric comparison to Python

takeaways.technique: Per-step model selection proven by evals
takeaways.what_they_do: Because each step is evaluated individually, prove the smallest adequate model per step (e.g., Nova Micro for a router) rather than one model for the whole pipeline.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can with an evaluation framework prove to yourself the smallest model that's appropriate to use on each step
